title: Juice it or lose it (talk)
description: Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho take a plain Breakout clone and keep layering feedback until it feels alive. The canonical demonstration of 'juice'.
pattern: Every game event (hit, bounce, spawn, destroy) should get several overlapping responses: an eased tween, a squash/stretch on the object, particles, a sound, and on big events a short screen shake. Bring objects in with ease-out or overshoot curves instead of popping them in. Effects stack, so add them in layers and keep a debug toggle per layer to compare with and without.

title: The Art of Screenshake (Jan Willem Nijman, Vlambeer)
description: INDIGO 2013 talk that turns a flat top-down shooter into a Vlambeer-style one through a few dozen small changes. Reference for shooter feel.
pattern: For shooters: make bullets big and fast, add a muzzle flash and a little random spread, flash enemies white on hit, knock them back, and push the player back a bit when firing. Freeze the game for a few frames on heavy hits (hitstop), leave shells and corpses on the floor, and lerp the camera toward where the player aims. Add screen shake last, scaled to the size of the event.

title: Math for Game Programmers: Juicing Your Cameras With Math (Squirrel Eiserloh, GDC 2016)
description: GDC talk on camera shake driven by a 'trauma' value and smooth noise, plus camera smoothing and framing. The source of the trauma-squared shake recipe.
pattern: Keep a trauma value in [0,1]; events add to it (e.g. +0.3 to +0.5) and it decays linearly over time (about 1 per second). Shake amount = trauma^2 (or ^3), so small hits barely shake and big ones shake hard. Offset = maxOffset * shake * noise(seed, t * freq) per axis, and angle = maxAngle * shake * noise(seed2, t); use smooth Perlin/simplex noise rather than random per frame, and favour rotation in 2D. Apply shake to a child of the follow camera so smoothing and shake stay separate.

title: Math for Game Programmers: Building a Better Jump (Kyle Pittman, GDC 2016)
description: Derives platformer jump gravity and launch speed from designer-facing numbers (height, distance, time) instead of tuning raw physics constants.
pattern: Pick jump height h and time to apex t_h (or horizontal distance to apex x_h at run speed v_x, so t_h = x_h / v_x). Then initial velocity v0 = 2h / t_h and gravity g = -2h / t_h^2. Use a larger gravity after the apex (a shorter descent time) for a snappier arc, and switch to that heavy gravity early when the button is released to get variable height. Integrate with velocity Verlet or a fixed step so the arc does not depend on frame rate.

title: Celeste Player.cs (official source excerpt)
description: Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry published Celeste's player controller as a learning resource. Read it for exact movement constants and the state machine of a celebrated platformer.
attribution: Maddy Thorson, Noel Berry (Extremely OK Games)
pattern: Units are pixels and seconds at 320x180: gravity 900, max fall 160 (fast-fall 240), max run 90, run accel 1000, run decel 400, air control multiplier 0.65. Jump speed 105 upward plus a 40 horizontal boost; holding jump sustains that speed for up to 0.2 s (VarJumpTime), and gravity is halved while |vy| < 40 with jump held, which rounds the apex. Coyote grace is 0.1 s; dash is 240 speed for 0.15 s, ending at 160, with climb stamina 110. The player is a state machine (normal, climb, dash, swim, etc.) with per-state update functions.
licence_note: MIT covers only the code in that repo, not the commercial game or its assets.

title: Coyote time and jump buffering
description: Two forgiveness timers that make platformer jumps feel responsive: allow a jump shortly after leaving a ledge, and remember a jump pressed shortly before landing.
pattern: Coyote time: while grounded, set graceTimer = 0.1 s; when airborne, count it down; a jump is legal if grounded or graceTimer > 0, and jumping zeroes the timer so it can't double-fire (Celeste uses exactly 0.1 s). Jump buffer: when jump is pressed, set bufferTimer to about 0.1 s; each frame, if bufferTimer > 0 and a jump is legal, jump and clear the buffer. Consume the buffered press on any action that uses it (jump, wall jump, super jump). Both timers should be measured in seconds, not frames.

title: Variable jump height
description: Let a tap give a short hop and a hold give a full jump. There are two common implementations: cut velocity on release, or sustain launch speed while held.
pattern: Method A (cut): on button release while rising, multiply vertical velocity by about 0.5 (or clamp it to a small upward value). Method B (sustain, Celeste): for up to 0.2 s after takeoff, while the button is held, keep vy at the launch speed; release or timeout ends it. Method C (Pittman): on release, switch to the heavier fall gravity. In every method, also apply a minimum hop so a one-frame tap still leaves the ground visibly.

title: Why Does Celeste Feel So Good to Play? (Game Maker's Toolkit)
description: Mark Brown breaks down Celeste's hidden assists and movement tuning: coyote time, buffering, corner correction, apex hang and more.
pattern: Hide generous assists where the player won't notice them: coyote time, jump buffering, nudging the player around ceiling corners when a jump clips an edge by a few pixels, and a floaty apex (half gravity near the top). Add squash on landing and stretch on takeoff, dust particles and hair colour as dash-state feedback. Tune for the player's intent, not literal input.

title: Game Feel (Steve Swink, book)
description: Book on the 'virtual sensation' of control: real-time control, simulated space and polish, with metrics for analysing how a game responds to input.
pattern: Game feel comes from three layers: real-time control (input to response with short latency), simulated space (collision and physics the player can feel against), and polish (effects that sell the interaction without changing the simulation). Keep input-to-visible-response within about 100 ms so control reads as instant. Measure feel with concrete parameters (acceleration, max speed, turn rate, apex time) and change one at a time.

title: Game Feel: The Secret Ingredient (Steve Swink, article)
description: Gamasutra/Game Developer article that introduced Swink's game-feel framework before the book.
pattern: Treat feel as a loop of intent, input, simulation response and perception. Fast, predictable response and readable physical context make control enjoyable even before content exists, so prototype and tune movement first. Polish (sound, particles, animation) amplifies feel but can't fix a sluggish control loop.

title: Scroll Back: The Theory and Practice of Cameras in Side-Scrollers (Itay Keren)
description: Catalogue of 2D camera techniques with examples from classic games: camera windows, snapping, smoothing, focus and framing tricks.
pattern: Use a camera window (dead zone box) horizontally so small moves don't scroll; vertically, snap only when the player lands on a platform so jumps don't bob the view. Smooth with lerp toward the target: per frame, pos += (target - pos) * (1 - exp(-k*dt)). Lead the player: keep more screen ahead in the facing or velocity direction (forward or projected focus), and let level 'cue' attractors pull the camera toward points of interest. For multiple players, average positions and zoom to fit.

title: Super Mario 3D World's 4 Step Level Design (Game Maker's Toolkit)
description: How Nintendo builds levels around one mechanic in four beats (kishōtenketsu): introduce, develop, twist, conclude.
pattern: Build each level around one new mechanic. Step 1: introduce it where failure is cheap. Step 2: develop it with harder layouts. Step 3: twist it, combining it with something else or changing its rules. Step 4: conclude with a short final test or celebration, then retire the mechanic so the next level can bring a new one.

title: Boss Keys (Game Maker's Toolkit series)
description: Mark Brown's series diagramming Zelda dungeons and Metroidvania maps as lock-and-key dependency graphs. Reference for dungeon and metroidvania structure.
pattern: Model the level as a graph whose nodes are rooms or regions and whose edges are gated by keys (items, switches or abilities). Keep it solvable: every lock's key must be reachable without that lock, which a breadth-first search over the graph can check. Metroidvanias use abilities as reusable keys, so one item opens many gates across the map; add one-way shortcuts back to hubs to reduce backtracking. Track how many locks are available at once: more open choices make it less linear.

title: What Makes a Good Puzzle? (Game Maker's Toolkit)
description: Mark Brown on puzzle design: the 'catch' (insight) at the heart of each puzzle, clear rules, and stripping noise.
pattern: Design each puzzle around one catch: a non-obvious consequence of known rules that the player has to realise. Make every rule visible and consistent, and remove pieces that don't serve the catch so trial and error doesn't beat insight. Good puzzles first invite a wrong assumption, then reward the player for questioning it.

title: Hexagonal Grids (Red Blob Games)
description: Amit Patel's interactive guide to hex grid coordinates, distances, neighbours, rings, line drawing, pixel conversion and storage.
pattern: Use cube coordinates (q, r, s) with q + r + s = 0, and store only axial (q, r). Distance = (|dq| + |dr| + |ds|) / 2; the six neighbours are fixed direction offsets. For pointy-top hexes, x = size * (sqrt(3) * q + sqrt(3)/2 * r) and y = size * 1.5 * r. Converting back from pixels gives fractional cube coordinates; round each component and reset the one with the largest rounding error so the sum stays 0.

title: Introduction to A* (Red Blob Games)
description: Interactive explanation of breadth-first search, Dijkstra's algorithm and A* on grids and graphs, with code.
pattern: Keep a frontier priority queue ordered by f = cost_so_far + heuristic, a came_from map and a cost_so_far map. Pop the lowest f, stop if it is the goal, and for each neighbour relax its cost if new_cost is lower. Use Manhattan distance on 4-way grids and octile distance on 8-way grids, never overestimating. Use BFS when all steps cost the same and Dijkstra when you need distances to many targets.

title: Flow Field Pathfinding for Tower Defense (Red Blob Games)
description: Shows how one breadth-first search from the goal gives every enemy a path, the standard tower-defence pathing trick.
pattern: Run one BFS (or Dijkstra for weighted terrain) outward from the goal over the whole grid to get a distance per tile, then store for each tile the neighbour with the smallest distance. Every enemy, however many, just steps toward its tile's arrow. Recompute when a tower is placed, and reject placements that would leave any spawn with no path (spawn distance becomes infinite).

title: Making maps with noise functions (Red Blob Games)
description: Generates terrain heightmaps, islands and biomes from layered noise, with interactive sliders.
pattern: Elevation = sum of noise octaves: amplitudes 1, 1/2, 1/4… at frequencies 1, 2, 4…, divided by the amplitude sum. Reshape with pow(e, exponent) to flatten valleys or sharpen peaks. Sample a second, independent noise for moisture and choose the biome from an (elevation, moisture) table. For islands, blend elevation with a function of distance from the centre so the edges sink below sea level.

title: Polygonal Map Generation for Games (Amit Patel)
description: Classic write-up of generating island maps from Voronoi polygons, with coastlines, elevation, rivers, moisture and biomes.
pattern: Scatter random points, relax them with one or two rounds of Lloyd's algorithm, and build the Voronoi polygons and their Delaunay dual as a graph. Mark land and water with a shape function (noise or radial), then set elevation by distance from the coast and redistribute it. Run rivers downhill from random high corners, set moisture by distance from fresh water, and pick biomes from elevation and moisture.

title: Game Programming Patterns: State (Robert Nystrom)
description: Free online book chapter on finite state machines for game entities, from enum-and-switch to state objects, hierarchical states and pushdown automata.
pattern: Replace tangled boolean flags (isJumping, isDucking…) with one current state. Each state handles input and update and decides the next state, with enter/exit hooks for animation and setup. Share behaviour with hierarchical states (an OnGround parent handles jump for Standing and Ducking), and use a stack (pushdown automaton) for temporary states like firing or pause that return to the previous one.
licence_note: Prose CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; code samples MIT.

title: Game Programming Patterns: Game Loop (Robert Nystrom)
description: Book chapter on structuring the main loop: variable, fixed and semi-fixed timesteps and decoupled rendering.
pattern: Each frame, add the real elapsed time to a lag accumulator; while lag >= MS_PER_UPDATE, run one fixed update and subtract. Then render with extrapolation or interpolation factor lag / MS_PER_UPDATE. This keeps simulation deterministic and stable across fast and slow machines.
licence_note: Prose CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; code samples MIT.

title: Game Programming Patterns: Component (Robert Nystrom)
description: Book chapter on splitting a monolithic entity class into components, the idea that ECS engines like Bevy take further.
pattern: Split an entity into independent components by domain (input, physics, graphics, audio) so each can be reused and changed alone. Components talk through shared state on the entity, direct references, or messages; prefer the least coupled option that works. In an ECS, components are plain data and systems hold the behaviour.
licence_note: Prose CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; code samples MIT.

title: Fix Your Timestep! (Glenn Fiedler)
description: Explains the accumulator loop for deterministic fixed-step physics with smooth interpolated rendering.
pattern: frameTime = now - last, clamped to about 0.25 s to avoid the spiral of death; accumulator += frameTime. While accumulator >= dt (e.g. 1/60 s): previous = current; integrate(current, dt); accumulator -= dt. Render lerp(previous, current, accumulator / dt). Physics then runs at the same rate on every machine, which is also what rollback netcode needs.

title: A Theory of Fun for Game Design (Raph Koster)
description: Book arguing that fun is the brain's enjoyment of learning and mastering patterns, and that games go stale once their patterns are fully grokked.
pattern: Treat the game as a set of patterns for the player to learn: fun peaks while they are learning and drops to boredom once a pattern is mastered, or to frustration if it can't be learned. Keep adding new patterns or deeper variations at a pace slightly ahead of the player's skill. Each system should teach something the player can get better at.
licence_note: The site describes the book; the thesis summary is from the book itself.

title: Valve Developer Community: Level Design category
description: Valve's wiki section of level design articles for Source/Hammer: scale, layout, lighting, gameplay flow and optimisation.
pattern: Build around fixed player metrics: in Half-Life 2 the player hull is 32x32x72 units and the step height is 18, so doors, stairs and cover come from those numbers. Guide the player with landmarks, light and sightlines rather than signs, and alternate tension and rest spaces. Block out with simple geometry and playtest before detailing.
licence_note: Wiki licence not confirmed (page 403 to fetcher; opened via HTTP).

title: WaveFunctionCollapse (Maxim Gumin)
description: Reference implementation of the WFC algorithm that generates bitmaps and tilemaps locally similar to an example, used widely for procedural levels.
pattern: Every output cell starts as the set of all allowed patterns (overlapping model: NxN patches from a sample, with their frequencies; tiled model: tiles plus adjacency rules). Repeat: pick the undecided cell with the lowest entropy, collapse it to one pattern chosen by weight, and propagate, removing incompatible options from neighbours until nothing changes. If a cell has no options left, restart (or backtrack). Seed the RNG for reproducible levels.

title: Rooms and Mazes: A Procedural Dungeon Generator (Bob Nystrom)
description: Dungeon generator that places rooms, fills the gaps with mazes, connects regions with a spanning tree plus a few loops, and trims dead ends.
pattern: Try N random room placements (odd sizes and positions), discarding any that overlap. Fill the remaining solid area with randomised flood-fill mazes, then find connector tiles between different regions. Grow a spanning tree from a random region by opening connectors, give each leftover connector a small chance (a few per cent) to open as well so the map has loops, and finally fill in dead ends repeatedly.

title: Spelunky Generator Lessons (Darius Kazemi)
description: Interactive breakdown of how Spelunky builds levels: a 4x4 room grid with a guaranteed solution path, then room templates.
pattern: Lay out a 4x4 grid of rooms. Start in a random top-row room and walk: roll 1-5, with 1-2 going left, 3-4 right and 5 down; hitting a side wall drops down a row. Room types encode exits (1: left/right, 2: plus bottom, 3: plus top), so dropping marks the room above as type 2 and the one below as type 2 or 3; leaving the bottom row places the exit. Fill the remaining cells with random side rooms, then build each room from hand-made templates that contain randomised obstacle chunks.

title: The Incredible Power of Dijkstra Maps (RogueBasin)
description: Roguelike AI technique: precomputed distance fields that monsters roll down, combined to express goals like chase, flee or seek items.
pattern: Set goal cells to 0 and all others to a large number, then relax repeatedly (each cell = min(neighbour) + 1) until stable; a monster moves to its lowest neighbour. For fleeing, multiply a chase map by about -1.2 and rescan so cornered monsters slip past instead of getting trapped. Sum several maps with weights (player, items, allies) to get desire-driven behaviour.

title: Berlin Interpretation (roguelike definition)
description: 2008 community definition of what makes a roguelike, with high- and low-value factors. Use it to scope roguelike vs roguelite loops.
pattern: Core roguelike: random level generation, permadeath, turn-based movement on a grid, one mode for all actions, complex interacting systems, resource management, combat and exploration. A roguelite keeps the run-and-die loop but adds meta-progression: currency earned in a run buys permanent unlocks between runs. Seed each run, save only between runs (or save-and-quit), and make a run 20-60 minutes long.

title: Roguelike Tutorial in Rust (Herbert Wolverson)
description: Huge free tutorial building a roguelike in Rust with an ECS: FOV, combat, items, save/load and many map generators.
pattern: Structure the game as an ECS with a run-state enum (AwaitingInput, PlayerTurn, MonsterTurn, ShowInventory…) driving which systems run. Map generators are interchangeable builders (BSP rooms, cellular automata caves, drunkard's walk, Voronoi, WFC) behind one interface, with a final pass that culls unreachable areas. Save by serialising the marked entities and components with serde.

title: Boids (Craig Reynolds)
description: The original flocking model: emergent group motion from three local steering rules.
pattern: Each agent looks only at neighbours within a radius (and optionally a view angle). Separation steers away from neighbours that are too close, alignment steers toward their average heading, and cohesion steers toward their average position. Sum the three with weights, clamp the steering force and the speed, and integrate; use a spatial hash so neighbour search is not O(n^2).

title: Easing Functions Cheat Sheet (easings.net)
description: Visual cheat sheet of the standard Penner-style easing curves with formulas, for tweens and UI motion.
pattern: A tween maps normalised time t in [0,1] to progress: value = a + (b - a) * ease(t). Use ease-out (e.g. easeOutCubic = 1 - (1 - t)^3) for things arriving, ease-in for things leaving, and easeOutBack (overshoot constant about 1.70158) for a playful pop. Keep UI tweens short (about 0.15-0.4 s) and drive them from game time so pause and slow motion work.
licence_note: The site's source is GPL-3.0; the formulas themselves are standard math.

title: The guide to implementing 2D platformers (Rodrigo Monteiro)
description: Compares four ways to build platformer physics (pure tile, smooth tile, bitmask, vector) and details slopes, one-way platforms and ladders.
pattern: Move one axis at a time, X then Y (X first if you have slopes), checking the tiles in the swept row or column and stopping at the nearest obstacle. A one-way platform blocks only on the Y axis and only if the player's feet were fully above it before the move. For slopes, compute the floor height under the player's centre column instead of using the tile's top edge, and stick to the slope when walking downhill. Ladders switch the character into a climbing state with gravity off.

title: Doing Thumbstick Dead Zones Right (Josh Sutphin)
description: Explains why per-axis dead zones feel bad and how a scaled radial dead zone fixes it. Essential for twin-stick and top-down shooters.
pattern: Don't zero each axis separately (axial dead zone): the stick snaps to the cardinal directions. Use a radial dead zone instead: if |v| < dz (about 0.2-0.25), output zero. Then rescale so output still starts at 0 just past the dead zone: out = normalize(v) * (|v| - dz) / (1 - dz). For twin-stick aiming, keep the last aim direction when the right stick is inside the dead zone.

title: The Math of Idle Games, Part I (Anthony Pecorella)
description: Kongregate's guide to the exponential cost and linear production formulas behind idle/incremental games, with bulk-buy formulas.
pattern: Cost of the next generator = base_cost * rate^owned (AdVenture Capitalist's lemonade stand uses rate 1.07 and base cost about 4). Production = base_production * owned * multipliers, so it grows linearly while cost grows exponentially, and periodic multiplier unlocks keep progress moving. The cost of buying n at once is base * rate^owned * (rate^n - 1) / (rate - 1); invert it with a log to find the most you can afford. Use big-number or log-scale storage once values pass about 1e15.

title: Slay the Spire: Metrics Driven Design and Balance (Anthony Giovannetti, GDC 2019)
description: How Mega Crit used play data from Early Access to balance a roguelike deckbuilder. Reference for the card battler loop.
pattern: Card battler loop (Slay the Spire's rules): draw 5 cards a turn, 3 energy to spend, unplayed cards are discarded, and the discard pile is shuffled back when the draw pile runs out. Enemies show their next action (intent), so each turn is a readable puzzle. After each fight offer a choice of 1 of 3 cards (or skip), and branch the map. Balance with telemetry: log pick rate and win rate per card and per floor, and adjust outliers.

title: Rhythm Quest Devlog 4: music synchronisation (DDRKirby(ISQ))
description: How a rhythm game keeps gameplay locked to the music: scheduled playback, mapping the audio clock to game time, latency calibration.
patterns: DSP clock to game clock regression
pattern: Schedule the song to start at a known future audio-clock time (about 1 s ahead) instead of 'play now'. Each frame, map the audio DSP clock to game time with a linear fit over the last ~15 samples, and never let song time go backwards. songTime = smoothedDspTime - scheduledStart - calibrationOffset (an example offset is 50 ms, set per device by the player). If it drifts more than about 50 ms from the audio source's reported position, resync.

title: Making Custom Car Physics in Unity (Toyful Games, Very Very Valet)
description: Video on arcade car handling built from one rigid body and a raycast per wheel, with suspension, steering grip and acceleration as separate forces.
pattern: Treat the car as one rigid body and cast a ray down from each wheel. Suspension force along the wheel's up axis = offset * stiffness - (velocity along up) * damping. Grip: take the wheel's sideways velocity, remove a fraction of it (the grip factor, lower for drift) as a force at the wheel. Acceleration applies force along the wheel's forward axis, scaled by a torque curve of normalised speed; steer by rotating the front wheels.

title: Keep Running: Procedural Level Generation in Sure Footing (Tommy Thompson)
description: Postmortem of an infinite runner's generator: action grammars mapped to hand-made platform chunks, with budgets that grow as you play.
pattern: Generate in two stages: first choose an abstract sequence of player actions (jump, drop, spring, fork) from a grammar, then map each action to a hand-built chunk that has a difficulty cost. Each stretch has a budget that caps total cost; relax the budget and unlock harder chunk sets as the run goes on. Separate stretches with rest pieces and use section transitions to switch visual mutators. Spawn ahead with triggers and despawn behind the player.

title: Vampire Survivors-like (genre)
description: Wikipedia overview of the 'bullet heaven' genre: move-only control against escalating hordes, with roguelike runs and periodic upgrades.
pattern: The player only moves; weapons fire on their own cooldowns. A spawn director places enemies in a ring just off-screen and raises spawn rate and enemy types on a timeline (Vampire Survivors stages run 30 minutes). Kills drop XP gems that are pulled in within a pickup radius; each level-up pauses and offers a choice of 3-4 upgrades (new weapon, weapon level, passive). Gold from runs buys permanent stat unlocks.
licence_note: The Wikipedia page covers waves and upgrades; the specific numbers come from common knowledge of the genre.

title: Tile-matching video game (match-3)
description: Wikipedia overview of tile-matching games (Bejeweled, Candy Crush): swap, match three or more, gravity, chain reactions, power-ups.
pattern: Swap two adjacent tiles and keep the swap only if it makes a line of 3 or more; otherwise animate it back. Resolve in a loop with input locked: clear the matches, let tiles above fall, spawn new tiles at the top, check for matches again, and award more points for each cascade step. Matches of 4 or 5, or L and T shapes, create special pieces (line clear, bomb, colour clear). After settling, if no valid move exists, reshuffle.

title: Procedural Landmass Generation (Sebastian Lague)
description: Tutorial series and MIT-licensed project for endless procedural terrain: octave noise heightmaps, falloff, mesh LOD and chunk streaming.
pattern: Heightmap = sum over octaves of noise(x * frequency) * amplitude, where frequency is multiplied by lacunarity (about 2) and amplitude by persistence (about 0.5) each octave; normalise and pass through a height curve. Subtract a falloff map for islands. Build meshes per chunk, choosing a coarser LOD step with distance, and generate chunks on worker threads as the viewer moves.
licence_note: Repo code MIT; the YouTube videos are all rights reserved.
